# Cook County Land Bank Authority (CCLBA) — Programs Research

**Research date:** September 2, 2026
**Source:** cookcountylandbank.org (live pages)
**Headline finding:** CCLBA does NOT call anything a literal "grant program" by name in its main navigation. The terminology is **Purchase Assistance Program**, funded out of the **Equity Fund**. Press coverage (Austin Weekly News, 10/3/2024) refers to it as "flexible $20,000 grants," so this is the program commonly meant by "the cook county land bank grant."

---

## MASTER LIST OF ALL CCLBA PROGRAMS (current navigation)

Per the site menu (Sept 2026) there are 5 buyer/developer-facing programs plus 2 operational categories:

| # | Program | Page |
|---|---------|------|
| 1 | **Purchase Assistance Program** (a.k.a. **Equity Fund Program**) — the "grant" | /equity-fund-program/ |
| 2 | **Homebuyer Direct Program** | /what-are-you-looking-for/homebuyer-direct-program/ |
| 3 | **Home Giveaway Program** | /homeownergiveaway/ |
| 4 | **Tax Certificate Program** | /taxcertificateprogram/ |
| 5 | **Residential/Community Developer** (property channel) | /what-are-you-looking-for/residential-community-developer/ |
| 6 | **Commercial/Industrial Property** (property channel) | /what-are-you-looking-for/commercial-industrial-property/ |
| 7 | **Donating/Conveying Property** (TO the Land Bank) | resources page |

There is NO traditional "grant" program. The Purchase Assistance Program is the only program that delivers cash to the buyer.

---

## 1. PURCHASE ASSISTANCE PROGRAM (Equity Fund) — THE "GRANT"

- **Status:** Open (rolling, first-come first-served, while funds last). Last updated 2026-07-28.
- **Description:** Cash assistance for owner-occupant buyers purchasing a CCLBA-listed home. Funded out of the Equity Fund.
- **Funding amount:** **6% of the purchase price, capped at $20,000.** Applied toward downpayment, closing costs, and pre-close costs (appraisal, insurance, inspection). Confirmed by Austin Weekly News (10/3/2024): "grants up to 6% of a home's purchase price, capped at $20,000."
- **Eligible buyer:** Any individual buyer — no income limits, no credit-score minimum imposed by CCLBA (lender rules apply).
- **Required buyer contribution:** Lesser of **$1,000 or 1%** of purchase price (cannot be gifted).
- **Eligible properties:** Must be on the published CCLBA "Eligible Purchase Assistance Properties" list (PDF updated periodically — 2025-08-05 version on site).
- **Occupancy:** Owner-occupied, **primary residence, 3-year minimum**. Buyer signs a Recapture Agreement at closing; if buyer violates (non-occupancy, sale, refinance for cash-out within 3 years) the grant is recaptured (forgiven pro-rata).
- **Layering:** Other grants / down-payment assistance are explicitly allowed.
- **Application package (all required):**
  1. Purchaser Assistance Program Checklist
  2. Completed Initial Application
  3. Notarized Occupancy Affidavit
  4. Buyer-Signed Recapture Agreement
  5. Fully executed contract (buyer + seller)
  6. Lender pre-approval (financed) or proof of funds within last 30–60 days (cash)
  7. Email complete package to **info@cookcountylandbank.org**
- **Processing time:** Up to **3 weeks** to receive award letter.
- **Homebuyer counseling:** Required for Land Bank-exclusive properties (work with participating Homebuyer Counseling Agencies).
- **Property condition:** Sold AS-IS. Buyer may pursue FHA 203K purchase-rehab loan.
- **Key URLs:**
  - Program parameters PDF: https://cookcountylandbank.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Equity-Fund-Home-Buyer-Direct-Grant-Program-3.11.2024.pdf
  - Eligible properties list: https://cookcountylandbank.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/CCLBA-Eligible-Purchase-Assistance-Properties_20250805.pdf
  - Recapture Agreement: https://cookcountylandbank.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Recapture-Agreement-Equity-Fund-6.2.2026-Sample.pdf

---

- **Status:** Open. Last updated 2026-03-17.
- **Description:** Buyers (or their brokers) apply directly to purchase a specific below-market, fixable home from CCLBA's inventory. Program launched 2017.
- **Eligible buyer:** Prospective owner-occupants. No income limit imposed by CCLBA. Down payment assistance is allowed from outside sources (lender, City of Chicago, Neighborhood Housing Services, IHDA, broker).

- **Multiple offers:** CCLBA weighs occupancy, contract contingencies, down payment, first-time homebuyer status.

# Design Decisions — Rental Tax Dashboard

## Architecture

**Single-page HTML + localStorage** — chosen because:
- No backend/server needed (runs entirely in browser)
- No data privacy concerns (data never leaves user's computer)
- Zero setup (open file in browser)
- Fully self-contained (no build tools, no npm)
- Data persists between sessions via localStorage

## Tech Stack Decisions

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| **Vanilla JS (no framework)** | Minimizes file size, no build step, easier maintenance |
| **Chart.js CDN** | Industry standard charting lib, small footprint, CDN-hosted |
| **Dark theme (slate/navy)** | Professional appearance, low eye strain for frequent use |
| **localStorage** | Browser-native, no backend, persists across sessions, ~5MB limit adequate |
| **Base64 receipt storage** | Simpler than IndexedDB for small files; 5MB limit noted in UI |
| **13 expense categories** | Mapped directly to IRS Schedule E line items for seamless tax prep |

## Why Not...

- **React/Vue/Svelte:** Overkill for this scope. Vanilla JS kept it under 65KB.
- **IndexedDB:** localStorage is simpler and sufficient for typical rental portfolios.
- **Server-side:** Adds deployment complexity, hosting costs, and data privacy concerns.
- **Multi-page app:** Single-page with tab navigation is snappier and keeps data access simple.

## Depreciation Calculation

Uses simplified straight-line calculation (Cost / Recovery Period). For Form 4562 purposes, this approximates the MACRS mid-month convention. Actual tax filing should use Form 4562 instructions for precise calculations including the first-year mid-month convention adjustment. The dashboard provides a close estimate intended for planning purposes.

# Notes — Methodology & Caveats

## Research Approach

Research was conducted by a delegated subagent that fetched content from IRS.gov via curl and browser navigation. All primary sources are IRS publications, topic pages, and tax forms. Secondary sources (BiggerPockets, Investopedia, Nolo) were cross-referenced but primary IRS sources took precedence.

## Key Caveats

### 1. Section 199A QBI — EXPIRATION RISK
The IRS QBI page (updated May 12, 2026) states the deduction applies to tax years "ending on or before December 31, 2025." Unless Congress enacted an extension between May and September 2026, this deduction is NOT available for tax year 2026. This is the single most important finding in the report.

### 2. TCJA Sunset — 2026 is a Transition Year
Many individual provisions of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act expired after December 31, 2025:
- Individual income tax rates revert to pre-TCJA levels
- Standard deduction roughly halves
- SALT deduction cap may be removed
- Personal exemptions return
- Pease limitation returns

### 3. No 2026 Inflation-Adjusted Figures
The IRS typically publishes tax-year inflation adjustments in October-November of the preceding year. As of this report date (September 2026), final 2026 figures for Section 179, excess business loss limits, and other inflation-indexed thresholds have not been confirmed. The report uses 2025 figures with explicit caveats.

### 4. Dashboard Mileage Rate
The 2026 standard mileage rate is estimated at $0.70/mile. The actual rate is established by the IRS annually (typically December). Update in the dashboard when the official rate is published.

### 3. Supporting Files
- `summary.md` — This file
- `notes.md` — Session notes and methodology
- `sources.json` — Structured source list
- `decisions.md` — Design decisions
- `run-log.md` — Execution log

## Critical 2026 Tax Caveats

1. **QBI Deduction (Section 199A):** Per IRS, applies to tax years ending on or before December 31, 2025. May NOT be available for 2026 unless Congress extended it.
2. **TCJA individual provisions sunset:** Many individual tax provisions expired after 2025 (rates, standard deduction, SALT cap). Verity current law before filing.
3. **2026 inflation-adjusted figures:** Most thresholds listed use 2025 IRS figures; 2026 figures TBD when IRS publishes them (typically October-November 2026).

## How to Use the Dashboard

1. Open `rental-tax-dashboard.html` in any modern browser
2. Add properties first (address, purchase details)
3. Record income, expenses, mileage, and capital assets throughout the year
4. Use the Tax Reports tab to generate Schedule E and Form 4562 summaries

All data stays in your browser's localStorage — no data leaves your computer.

# Cadence vs Synopsys Investment Analysis — Decisions

## Primary verdict
**Prefer Synopsys (SNPS) over Cadence (CDNS) for a fresh 2–5 year investment today.**

## Why SNPS wins
1. **Broader platform moat**
   - Synopsys is positioned across EDA, silicon IP, and now simulation/analysis after Ansys.
   - That expands wallet share and increases switching costs across the silicon-to-systems stack.

2. **AI complexity is a bigger monetization lever**
   - AI chips, chiplets, high-bandwidth memory integration, packaging, power integrity, and physical AI all favor more tools per design cycle.
   - Synopsys is well positioned to monetize that broader complexity.

3. **Valuation is more attractive on a forward non-GAAP basis**
   - Cadence looks cleaner, but also pricier relative to its forward earnings power.
   - Synopsys currently offers stronger modeled upside from the present price.

4. **Ansys creates a strategic edge if integration succeeds**
   - The acquisition is not just additive revenue; it materially expands the category the company can own.
   - If management executes, Synopsys can become the default engineering software layer from chip design through multiphysics validation.

## Why not make CDNS the top pick
- Cadence is still a high-quality compounder and arguably the cleaner operator today.
- However, the current valuation leaves less room for error.
- Its narrower scope versus Synopsys also limits the size of the strategic upside if system-level simulation becomes a larger part of engineering budgets.

## What would change the verdict
- If Synopsys stumbles on Ansys integration, margin recovery, or export restrictions intensify, the gap narrows materially.
- If Cadence compounds backlog into sustained 20%+ EPS growth while maintaining premium margins, CDNS could outperform despite the richer multiple.

## Bottom line

The seller is marketing the property at **$875,000** with an **ARV of $1,350,000** and **estimated repairs of $137,160**. ## Subject property facts

- Forward geocode labels the corridor as **Edgewater**.

### Why the location matters
- **Edgewater Park** is about **2.4 km / 1.5 mi / 5.6 min drive** away.

# Uber Vehicle Arbitrage Deep Dive — Summary

**Session:** uber-vehicle-arbitrage-deep-dive  
**Date:** 2026-08-05  
**Source:** Discord

## Executive verdict
Uber vehicle arbitrage is **real**, but there are **two very different businesses** hiding under the same phrase:

1. **Driver-side arbitrage** — you rent a car, then try to earn more on Uber than the rental + operating costs.
2. **Owner-side arbitrage** — you own/control vehicles and rent them to Uber drivers at a spread.

### Bottom line
- **Driver-side:** viable as a short-term bridge, test, or emergency fallback. It is **not** great as a long-term wealth strategy unless your market/hourly gross is strong.
- **Owner-side:** this is the actual arbitrage business. It can work, but only with tight controls on **vehicle acquisition price, utilization, insurance, maintenance, and claims**.
- **Best interpretation:** Uber vehicle arbitrage is **more operations business than passive income**. If you want scale, think **fleet management**, not side hustle.

---

## What the research shows

### Official Uber signal
Uber explicitly supports the entry path for drivers who do not own a qualified car:
- Uber’s Vehicle Marketplace says drivers can **rent or buy a car for rideshare** through partner options.
- Uber’s driver requirements page says new drivers must generally:
  - meet minimum age requirements,
  - have licensed driving experience,
  - use an eligible 4-door vehicle,
  - provide license/documents,
  - pass screening,
  - and can also **rent or lease a car** through Uber-linked options.

### Market/community signal
Collected social/community evidence was directionally consistent:
- Many drivers say rental economics feel tight because Uber pay is volatile and platform take rates feel high.
- At the same time, examples still exist of peer fleet owners renting cars to Uber drivers for around **$350/week**.
- Third-party rideshare rental reviews still show examples like a **2020 Toyota Corolla around $375/week all-in** on older HyreCar-style marketplace economics.
- Market structure appears to be consolidating: third-party coverage indicates **HyreCar and Getaround shut down**, which suggests the easy “list your car anywhere” era is weaker than before.

---

## The 2 business models

## 1) Driver-side Uber rental arbitrage
This is the simplest way to start.

### How it works
- You do **not** own the car.
- You get a rideshare-eligible vehicle through Uber’s rental marketplace or another provider.
- You drive enough to cover:
  - weekly rental,
  - gas/charging,
  - tolls/washes/misc,
  - then keep the remainder.

### Who this works for
- Someone without a qualifying car
- Someone testing Uber before buying a vehicle
- Someone replacing income while their own car is in the shop
- Someone entering a high-demand market temporarily

### Pros
- Fastest start
- No long-term car debt up front
- No depreciation on your own personal vehicle
- Can validate your market before making a bigger move

### Cons
- Thin margins if gross earnings are mediocre
- You carry the scheduling risk: if you don’t drive, rent still hits
- Accident/downtime can wipe out a week
- Long-term, you are paying retail access prices for the car

---

## 2) Owner-side / fleet-side Uber vehicle arbitrage
This is the real business model if you mean “vehicle arbitrage.”

### How it works
- You acquire vehicles cheaply enough that the weekly rent to drivers creates a spread.
- You rent the cars to screened Uber/Lyft/gig drivers.
- Your profit comes from the gap between:
  - **weekly rent collected**, and
  - **all-in monthly ownership + operating cost**.

### Revenue engine
Typical owner-side spread drivers:
- low acquisition cost
- high utilization (cars on rent most weeks)
- solid maintenance discipline
- good driver screening
- minimal idle downtime between renters

### What kills the model
- overpaying for cars
- bad renters
- claims headaches
- mechanical downtime
- weak insurance setup
- idle cars sitting unrented

---

## Step-by-step: how to get started

## Path A — start as a driver/renter
1. **Check city eligibility**
   - Verify your city’s Uber driver and vehicle requirements.
2. **Apply to drive**
   - License, screening, profile, local documentation.
3. **Source a vehicle**
   - Uber Vehicle Marketplace first.
   - Compare weekly all-in cost, mileage terms, deposit, insurance, maintenance responsibility.
4. **Model your weekly break-even**
   - If you can’t comfortably clear rent + energy + your target income, don’t start.
5. **Run a 2–4 week test**
   - Track gross per hour, trip density, airport/wait time, peak windows, fuel cost.
6. **Decision gate**
   - If market is weak, stop.
   - If market is strong, either continue short-term or transition into owning a vehicle.

## Path B — start as a small fleet owner
1. **Pick a city and product**
   - Economy rideshare cars first. Avoid fancy vehicles early.
2. **Choose your legal/operating setup**
   - LLC, business banking, bookkeepin

- disciplined bidding,
- well-developed estimating processes,
- effective project controls, and
- reliable forecasting,

## Methodology
- **Scoring:** 1-5 rating on two axes (Regulatory Friendliness × Income Potential)
- **Regulatory scoring factors:** STR permit requirements, caps, minimum stays, owner-occupancy, state preemption
- **Income scoring factors:** Tourist volume, nightly rates, occupancy %, seasonal patterns

1. Must have minimal or no STR-specific restrictions (score 4+ on regulatory)

- Used Zillapi MCP for real property-level data where possible
- Supplemented with knowledge of regulations and market dynamics
- STR income estimates derived by applying a 2-3x multiplier to long-term rent zestimate based on industry benchmarks for beach/resort markets

- Summary report provides actionable, ranked recommendations

- Regulation data organized by state vs. city to help identify broader opportunity zones
